Section 01

Plain-English Summary

Read this section first — it tells you everything you need to know without any technical language.

⚡ The Most Important Finding: Four of our eight products are currently overpriced relative to where demand is highest. Adjusting prices to their modelled optimum could increase total daily portfolio profit by an estimated £572 — or approximately £208,649 per year.

What We Did

We analysed 5,840 daily pricing observations across eight products over two years. For each day, we had the product's price, competitor prices, marketing spend, product visibility, discount rate, and how many units were actually sold. We used this data to build a machine learning model that predicts demand at any given price — and then used that model to find the price that maximises profit for each product.

The original products and their pricing structures are fully preserved; three new complementary products were added to provide greater category diversity and modelling depth.
Section 02

The Business Problem — Why Pricing Matters

The Challenge of E-Commerce Pricing

Pricing is one of the most powerful levers in e-commerce — and one of the most difficult to get right. Set your price too high and customers buy from a competitor. Set it too low and you leave money on the table. The optimal price sits in between: high enough to protect margin, low enough to maintain demand. Finding that point — and keeping it updated as market conditions change — is what this project addresses.

💡 The Three Pricing Questions This Report Answers

1. How sensitive is demand to price changes? (Price elasticity analysis)
2. What price maximises profit for each product? (Optimisation model)
3. What happens to the portfolio if we move prices up or down? (Scenario testing)

Why This Is Hard Without Data

Without data, pricing decisions rely on gut feel, competitor copying, or simple cost-plus rules. These approaches miss crucial information: that different customers respond differently to price changes, that demand varies by season and day of week, and that the relationship between price and sales is rarely linear. A data-driven model captures all of these effects simultaneously.

Section 04

Exploring the Data — What Patterns Did We Find?

FIG 01

E-Commerce Pricing Overview — Revenue, Demand, Discounts, and Seasonality

Top row: Revenue by product, price vs units sold scatter, and revenue share by category. Middle row: Daily revenue trend over two years with holiday peaks marked, discount rate distribution, and price positioning vs competitor. Bottom row: Marketing spend vs revenue relationship, and weekend vs weekday performance comparison.

Key Findings from the Data

GammaBand and ThetaMat dominate revenue — together accounting for the majority of total sales. These high-volume, lower-priced products are the most sensitive to price changes and deserve the most careful pricing attention.

Holiday periods generate dramatically higher revenue. Black Friday and Christmas windows show clear spikes in the trend line. Dynamic pricing — raising prices slightly during peak periods when demand is inelastic — is a clear opportunity.

Most products are priced within 10–20% of competitor levels, but there are periods of significant over- and under-pricing that damage either margin or volume. Tighter competitor monitoring and faster price adjustments could close this gap.

Marketing spend has a positive but modest correlation with revenue (r ≈ 0.35). This suggests diminishing returns at higher spend levels — targeting spend toward high-elasticity products during peak periods is the highest-leverage allocation.

Section 05

Price Sensitivity — How Customers Respond to Price Changes

Price elasticity measures how much demand changes when price changes. An elasticity of −2.0 means that a 10% price increase leads to a 20% drop in units sold. The higher the absolute value, the more sensitive customers are to price.

💡 What Elasticity Means in Practice

If elasticity is −3.0 (ThetaMat): raising the price by 10% cuts demand by 30%. You sell far fewer units and end up with less total revenue. You need to lower the price to grow profit.

If elasticity is −1.4 (DeltaDock): raising the price by 10% only cuts demand by 14%. Revenue goes up because the price increase more than offsets the lost volume. You can safely charge more.

Section 06

How the Models Work

We trained three machine learning models to predict how many units will sell at any given price, given all other conditions. We then used those predictions to find the price point that maximises profit for each product.

ModelPlain-English ExplanationWhy We Included It
Ridge Regression A linear model that finds the best-fit straight-line relationship between features and demand Transparent baseline; good for understanding linear price-demand relationships
Random Forest Hundreds of decision trees that vote together — handles complex, non-linear patterns well Robust to outliers; captures interaction effects between price, marketing, and seasonality
Gradient Boosting Trees that learn from each other's mistakes — the most powerful technique for structured data Best overall performance; used as the final model for all price recommendations

Validation Strategy

We split the data into training (75%), validation (10%), and test (15%) sets. The test set was held completely separate until final evaluation, giving an honest measure of how well the model predicts demand on days it has never seen before. All preprocessing — scaling, encoding — was applied to training data first, then identically applied to the test set to prevent data leakage.

Key Evaluation Metrics

MetricWhat It MeasuresWhy It Matters Here
R²How much of the variation in sales the model explainsHigher is better — 1.0 = perfect, 0.0 = no better than guessing the average
RMSEAverage error in units — how far off predictions typically areLower is better — in the same units as sales volume
MAEAverage absolute error in units (less sensitive to outliers)Useful for understanding typical day-to-day prediction accuracy
MAPEAverage percentage error — scale-independent accuracy measureAllows fair comparison across products with different sales volumes

The Gradient Boosting model explains 87.6% of the variation in daily sales volume, with an average prediction error of around 7.7 units per day. For lower-volume products like DeltaDock, the percentage error is higher — recommendations for these products should be treated as directional rather than precise.

Section 09

Scenario Testing — What If We Change Prices?

FIG 03

Pricing Strategy Analysis — Scenario Simulation, Feature Importance, and Seasonal Patterns

Top left: Current vs optimal vs competitor prices for each product with change annotation. Top right: Profit uplift vs price sensitivity — showing which products offer the biggest gains. Middle left: Portfolio profit under five pricing scenarios — from −20% to +20% across all products. Middle right: Feature importance showing which factors the model relies on most. Bottom row: Holiday vs normal day revenue, discount rate vs volume, and seasonal revenue heatmap by category.

The Scenario Results Tell a Clear Story

Increasing prices uniformly across the portfolio by 10% or 20% reduces total profit — because the high-elasticity products (GammaBand, ThetaMat, BetaBuds, ZetaHub) lose so much volume that the margin gain is more than offset. Conversely, reducing prices by 10% increases volume but not enough to compensate for the margin compression on lower-elasticity products.

💡 The Key Insight from Scenario Testing

Uniform price changes across the whole portfolio are almost never optimal. The right strategy is product-by-product optimisation: reduce prices on high-elasticity products (where volume gains more than compensate for the lower margin) and increase prices on low-elasticity products (where demand is sticky and margin can improve).

Holiday Pricing Opportunity

Holiday periods generate significantly higher revenue than normal days. During these windows, demand is typically less sensitive to price — customers are buying gifts and have already decided to purchase. This is a strong signal to maintain or slightly increase list prices during peak periods rather than running discounts, which give away margin unnecessarily when customers would buy anyway.

Section 10

Practical Recommendations

Immediate Pricing Changes (High Confidence)

  • Reduce BetaBuds price from current ~£53 to approximately £43. With elasticity of −2.65, the volume gain from a 19% reduction more than compensates for the lower per-unit margin. Estimated profit uplift: +69.8% daily.
  • Reduce ThetaMat price toward £27. This is the most elastic product in the portfolio — highly price-sensitive customers will respond strongly to a reduction. Estimated uplift: +38.4% daily.
  • Reduce GammaBand price toward £33. Already the highest-volume product, it has significant elasticity that makes lower pricing more profitable than current levels.
  • Increase DeltaDock price toward £81. With the lowest elasticity in the portfolio (−1.40), customers are relatively insensitive to higher prices on this product. This is underpriced relative to its demand characteristics.

Strategic Pricing Improvements

  • Implement dynamic pricing for holiday periods. During Black Friday, Christmas, and other peak windows, maintain or slightly raise list prices rather than discounting. Customers are buying regardless — discounts in this window give away margin unnecessarily.
  • Reduce discount frequency for low-elasticity products (DeltaDock, EtaDesk). These customers are less price-sensitive and do not need promotional incentives to purchase. Reserve discounts for high-elasticity products where they genuinely drive incremental volume.
  • Monitor competitor prices more frequently. The data shows periods of significant price gaps versus the market — both too high (which suppresses demand) and too low (which leaves margin behind). A price monitoring tool or alert system would help close these gaps faster.
  • Allocate marketing spend toward high-elasticity products during non-peak periods. The data shows that marketing spend has a positive correlation with demand — directing more spend toward products where demand is elastic maximises the return on marketing investment.

Longer-Term Pricing Intelligence

  • Build a live repricing pipeline that runs the model weekly on fresh sales data and flags products where current prices have drifted more than 10% from their modelled optimum.
  • If customer-level data becomes available, segment pricing analysis by customer cohort — new vs returning, high-value vs low-value — to explore whether different customer groups warrant different pricing strategies.
  • A/B test the recommended price changes before full rollout. Change the price for one product at a time, run it for 3–4 weeks, and measure the actual change in profit vs the control period before applying recommendations portfolio-wide.
Section 11

Limitations and Next Steps

What This Model Cannot Do

Causation vs correlation: The model identifies statistical relationships between price and demand. It cannot fully account for confounding factors — for example, periods of high marketing spend and low prices happening simultaneously make it harder to separate the individual effects of each.

Competitor reactions: The optimisation assumes competitors hold their prices steady. In practice, if we reduce prices aggressively, competitors may match or undercut, changing the demand landscape the model was trained on.

Long-run vs short-run effects: The model captures short-run price sensitivity. Brand perception and customer loyalty effects from sustained pricing strategies are harder to capture with daily sales data.

What More Data Would Improve

  • Customer-level data — conversion rates, basket size, repeat purchase rates — would allow demand modelling at the customer segment level rather than product level.
  • Real-time competitor price tracking at the SKU level would allow the model to incorporate relative price positioning as a live signal rather than a historical average.
  • Inventory and stock-out data — prices should be optimised jointly with inventory strategy, since running out of stock during peak demand periods is a direct revenue loss.
  • Customer review and return rate data — quality signals affect price tolerance and should be incorporated in a comprehensive pricing model.
✅ Recommended First Step: Begin with BetaBuds and ThetaMat — the two products with the largest modelled profit uplift from price reduction. Run a controlled 30-day test: reduce each product's price toward the recommended optimum and measure the actual change in daily profit. If results are consistent with model predictions, roll out the full portfolio optimisation.
